questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The right to receive information
questions.learningObjective: Describe the general principle of public access
questions.stem: Study card 1 asks what the public right to receive information about government means. Which statement best describes it?

options.text: Information held by the government is generally available unless a lawful basis withholds it
Only records that a citizen requests in writing are ever subject to the right
options.misconception: limits the right to formal written requests

options.text: Information may be withheld whenever disclosure might cause embarrassment to the agency
options.misconception: treats embarrassment as a lawful ground for withholding

options.text: The right applies to private records held by businesses doing work for the city
options.misconception: extends the right to private commercial records

questions.explanation: Public access principles begin from a presumption that government records are open, turning on recognised exceptions for privacy, safety, and law enforcement. The framing shows the default is disclosure.
questions.hint: Start from the default and look for exceptions.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Openness of criminal trials
questions.learningObjective: Interpret data on open and closed proceedings
questions.stem: Study card 2 tabulates public attendance at twelve trials, separating open proceedings from those closed by order. What does the table support?

options.text: That trials in this court are closed as a matter of routine practice
options.misconception: reads a few closures as a general practice

options.text: That public attendance is unrelated to whether proceedings are open
options.misconception: denies the relevance of attendance data

options.text: That closure is an exception requiring justification, since it applied to only a few cases
That attendance rose because the public preferred cases with fewer witnesses
options.misconception: invents a causal story the table cannot support

questions.explanation: Criminal proceedings are open by default and closure is the exception that must be justified, so mostly open trials in the table match the presumption. Attendance figures alone do not explain any single closure.
questions.hint: Ask whether closure is the rule or the exception.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The particularity a warrant must have
questions.learningObjective: Identify a defective warrant on a review chart
questions.stem: Study card 3 draws a warrant review: first whether the place is described with precision, then whether the items are identified, then whether the basis is stated. Which branch identifies a defective warrant?

options.text: The branch where the warrant names every room but names no items
options.misconception: assumes naming the place cures missing item descriptions

options.text: The branch where the warrant describes a place vaguely and names no specific items
The branch where the warrant names the place but omits the facts supporting the belief
options.misconception: believes describing the place alone satisfies the warrant

options.text: The branch where the warrant lists items but says nothing about who asked
options.misconception: treats the identity of the applicant as a required element

questions.explanation: A warrant must describe with particularity where to search and what to seize, and omitting either leaves officers without a defined scope. The branch naming both place and items together is the defective one.
questions.hint: Check both place and items for precision.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Voluntariness of consent to search
questions.learningObjective: Explain how voluntariness of consent is evaluated
questions.stem: Study card 4 covers a suspect who was told that refusing to consent would be used against him at sentencing. Explain how a court evaluates whether the consent was voluntary.

answer.exemplar: A court asks whether the consent was a product of coercion rather than a free and deliberate choice. The voluntariness inquiry weighs the suspect condition, the nature and duration of the questioning, the presence of advisements of rights, and the length of any detention, and it is not a question of whether the suspect simply felt that refusing was unwise.

questions.explanation: Consent is involuntary when police coercion overbore the suspect will, and the inquiry is objective rather than a test of subjective comfort. A threat linking refusal to sentencing bears on that question.
questions.hint: Focus on coercion and the totality of the encounter.

questions.topic: Searching a vehicle without a warrant
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of warrantless vehicle searches
questions.stem: Study card 5 records 200 vehicle searches: 60 made after an arrest of an occupant, 90 made on a probable cause basis, and 50 made with a warrant. What percentage of the searches were made without a warrant?
questions.explanation: Sixty plus 90 equals 150 warrantless searches, and 150 divided by 200 equals 0.75, so 75 percent. The count shows how much of the practice rests on exceptions rather than warrants.
questions.hint: Add the two warrantless categories, then divide by the total.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The fruit of the poisonous tree and its exceptions
questions.learningObjective: Determine the status of evidence derived from a defective warrant

stimulus.body: Officers entered the apartment under a warrant later found defective because the affidavit relied on a tip from an anonymous informant with no basis of knowledge. The officers searched a locked suitcase and found a ledger. The prosecutor proposes to use the ledger at trial.

questions.stem: Study card 6 attaches this log to the case file. What is the likely status of the ledger?

options.text: Admissible, because the officers acted in good faith on the warrant
options.misconception: assumes good faith cures every defective warrant

options.text: Admissible, because the suitcase was closed rather than open on the table
options.misconception: believes container closure removes the protection

options.text: Admissible, because the information came from a confidential informant
options.misconception: confuses informant credibility with the fruit doctrine

options.text: Suppressed, because it is the fruit of a search that violated the defendant rights

questions.explanation: The exclusionary rule bars evidence derived from an unconstitutional search, so the ledger must be excluded unless an exception applies. The facts show a warrant with no supporting basis and no good faith available.
questions.hint: Ask what produced the ledger and why the warrant failed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Reliance on a defective warrant
questions.learningObjective: Apply good faith reliance to an officer statement

stimulus.body: I read the warrant carefully, it named the second floor apartment and the filing cabinets in the back room, and I had no reason to think the magistrate had made any error. I searched only the places the warrant described.

questions.stem: Study card 7 pairs this statement with the warrant and the magistrate findings. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text: The evidence is excluded because the magistrate finding was plainly wrong
options.misconception: ignores the good faith reliance exception

options.text: The evidence is admissible because the officer reasonably relied on the warrant
The evidence is excluded because any warrant defect defeats the search
options.misconception: assumes warrantless suppression without exception

options.text: The evidence is admissible because the officer testimony establishes the facts
options.misconception: treats testimony as a substitute for the warrant

questions.explanation: An officer who reasonably relies on a warrant that later proves defective keeps the evidence admissible under the good faith exception. The card describes exactly that reliance, with no reason to doubt it.
questions.hint: Consider the officer reliance and its reasonableness.

questions.topic: Expectation of privacy in an observation
questions.learningObjective: Compare two surveillance methods
questions.stem: Study card 8 compares an officer watching a back alley from a public rooftop with one aiming a thermal camera at a window from a helicopter. Which comparison best reflects the analysis?

options.text: Both are lawful because officers may observe anything visible from a public vantage point
options.misconception: assumes altitude does not change the analysis

options.text: Both intrude because any surveillance of a home is a search
options.misconception: treats all observation of a home as a search

options.text: The rooftop watch intrudes because it is surveillance, while the helicopter does not
options.misconception: reverses the sense of intrusion in each case

options.text: The rooftop watch likely sees no protected area, while the aerial device may intrude on a home

questions.explanation: Observation of what is exposed to public view is not a search, but a dwelling receives strong protection and technology used to peer into a home may intrude. The two scenarios turn on that distinction.
questions.hint: Ask what part of the home the technology reaches.

questions.topic: The right to receive information
questions.learningObjective: Compare two records requests under access principles
questions.stem: Study card 9 presents two records requests. First, a request for the total budget of a city department. Second, a request for the personal home addresses of every employee. Which request is most likely to be granted?

options.text: The first, because budget records carry no personal privacy interest
Both, because any document held by the government is subject to disclosure
options.misconception: ignores recognised exceptions to disclosure

options.text: The second, because employee addresses help the public monitor government
options.misconception: invents a monitoring interest in home addresses

options.text: Neither, because the right to receive information never covers records requests
options.misconception: denies the request-based route to disclosure

questions.explanation: Budget records are public business carrying no privacy interest, while employee home addresses are personal data that exceptions protect. The first request fits the general presumption of access.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Openness of criminal trials
questions.learningObjective: State the requirements for closing a trial
questions.stem: Study card 10 concerns a judge who closed a trial to protect a cooperating witness. Which requirement governs that closure?

options.text: The closure must be approved by unanimous agreement of the jury
options.misconception: invents a jury vote requirement for closure

options.text: The closure is valid whenever a witness asks the court to protect them
options.misconception: treats a request alone as sufficient justification

options.text: The closure must be narrowly tailored to a compelling need, with a stated finding supporting it
The closure is valid if the public could hear the evidence through a transcript
options.misconception: treats a transcript substitute as always adequate

questions.explanation: Closing a criminal trial is disfavored and requires a finding that an exceptional need outweighs the public interest, plus narrow tailoring. A witness request and a later transcript do not meet that standard.
questions.hint: Ask about findings and narrow tailoring.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret data on how warrants describe a place
questions.stem: Study card 11 lists ninety search warrants and notes for each whether the place was described by street address, by general description, or not at all. What does the table show?

options.text: That a substantial number relied on general descriptions rather than fixed addresses
That all warrants were adequate because the issuing judge reviewed each one
options.misconception: assumes judicial review cures every defect

options.text: That the search warrant requirement is effectively meaningless in practice
options.misconception: generalizes from a portion of the sample

options.text: That particularity requirements vary deliberately from one judge to another
options.misconception: infers a deliberate variation the table cannot show

questions.topic: Voluntariness of consent to search
questions.learningObjective: Follow a consent flowchart to a valid search
questions.stem: Study card 12 draws a consent flowchart: first whether the consent was given, then whether it was voluntary, then whether the search stayed within the consent scope. Which branch indicates a valid search?

options.text: The branch where consent was given and officers searched everything they wanted
options.misconception: treats any written consent as unlimited authority

options.text: The branch where consent was voluntary and the officers stayed within its limits
The branch where consent was voluntary but the search exceeded what was asked
options.misconception: confuses scope of consent with voluntariness

options.text: The branch where no consent existed but the person was arrested nearby
options.misconception: substitutes arrest authority for consent analysis

questions.explanation: A consent search is valid only when consent is voluntary and the search stays within its scope. The middle branch shows valid consent exceeded by the search, which the consent itself does not allow.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Searching a vehicle without a warrant
questions.learningObjective: Explain the search incident to arrest rule
questions.stem: Study card 13 covers a search of a car after its driver was arrested for an outstanding warrant. Explain the rule that governs the search.

answer.exemplar: The automobile exception permits officers to search a vehicle when they have probable cause to believe the vehicle contains evidence of a crime, contraband, or the fruits of a crime, and the search is permissible because the mobility of a vehicle creates a real risk that evidence will disappear before a warrant can be obtained.

questions.explanation: A search incident to arrest for an outstanding warrant permits searching the passenger compartment for evidence of that crime without a separate warrant. The car mobility is the reason the exception exists.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrest itself establishes.

questions.topic: Reliance on a defective warrant
questions.learningObjective: Infer warrant preparation from a magistrate email

stimulus.body: Please confirm that the address in the warrant matches the apartment from the application, and that the affidavit states a basis for the belief that evidence will be found there. I want the file to reflect the source of the information rather than only the conclusion.

questions.stem: Study card 15 places this email in the file. What does it indicate about the warrant preparation?

options.text: The magistrate assumed the facts in the affidavit were true
options.misconception: reads a verification request as a factual assumption

options.text: The magistrate rejected the application because the address did not match
options.misconception: assumes the request was a denial

options.text: The magistrate required a stated source, which supports the warrant particularity and validity
The magistrate intended to add a second address to the warrant
options.misconception: invents an intention the email never states

questions.explanation: The magistrate asked for the address to match and for the affidavit to state its source, which is the review supporting particularity and validity. The email shows careful preparation rather than adoption of conclusions.
questions.hint: Read what the magistrate required before signing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Expectation of privacy in an observation
questions.learningObjective: Classify an observation as a search or not

stimulus.body: While standing on the public sidewalk at 2 a.m., I observed the suspect standing in the second-floor window of the apartment across the street, holding a large box, and waving. The room was lit by a lamp and I could see the person face clearly without any device.

questions.stem: Study card 16 treats this note as an observation rather than a search. Which statement best describes the analysis?

options.text: The search is lawful only because the officer had an arrest warrant for the suspect
options.misconception: makes an arrest warrant the basis for observation

options.text: The observation is unlawful because it occurred after midnight
options.misconception: treats the hour of the night as decisive

options.text: The observation required a warrant because it occurred inside a residence
options.misconception: confuses the location of the person with the intrusion

options.text: No reasonable expectation of privacy attaches to what is plainly visible from a public street

questions.explanation: The activity observed was exposed to public view from a public place, so no reasonable expectation of privacy attached and no warrant was needed. The room location inside a residence does not convert observation into intrusion.
questions.hint: Ask what the observer could plainly see.

questions.topic: The right to receive information
questions.learningObjective: Compare access to police reports and informant files
questions.stem: Study card 17 compares access to police reports and access to a confidential informant file. Which comparison best reflects the framework?

options.text: Both are closed because law enforcement records are exempt from public access
options.misconception: assumes a blanket exemption for police reports

options.text: Both are presumptively open, but law enforcement and privacy exceptions apply in each case
The police report is open and the informant file is closed in every case
options.misconception: states exceptions as automatic outcomes

options.text: Both are open because no public interest ever supports keeping records secret
options.misconception: denies that exceptions serve any public interest

questions.hint: Begin with openness, then look for exceptions.

questions.topic: Openness of criminal trials
questions.learningObjective: Identify the decisive step in a closure dispute
questions.stem: Study card 18 offers two facts about a trial. First, the prosecution moved to seal the witness list. Second, the defense stated an interest in cross-examining witnesses publicly. Which step decides the issue?

options.text: Whether the prosecutor preferred to avoid disclosing the witness identities
options.misconception: grounds the outcome in official preference

options.text: Whether the defense would have shown any prejudice from an open hearing
options.misconception: treats the defense showing as the only question

options.text: Whether the witness list can be provided to the public in redacted form later
options.misconception: assumes a later remedy always cures a closure

options.text: Whether sealing is narrowly tailored to a compelling need, weighed against the public interest

questions.explanation: The court weighs the public right to attend against a demonstrated need for closure, and the defense interest in open cross-examination is part of the balance. The inquiry is about narrow tailoring, not preference.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the defective feature of a warrant clause
questions.stem: Study card 19 describes a warrant to search the second floor of a building for every item bearing a particular brand. Which feature is most troubling?

options.text: The description gives no way to tell officers which objects fall within its scope
The warrant permits only a floor to be searched rather than a room
options.misconception: insists on room level detail in every case

options.text: The warrant names a brand rather than a category of evidence
options.misconception: treats brand identification as inherently vague

options.text: The warrant allows a search of a building rather than a dwelling
options.misconception: assumes only homes may be searched by warrant

questions.explanation: Particularity requires a description detailed enough that officers can tell what falls within the warrant scope. The brand standard gives no such guidance, which is the defect that matters.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The fruit of the poisonous tree and its exceptions
questions.learningObjective: Explain the independent source and inevitable discovery exceptions
questions.stem: Study card 22 asks about exceptions to the exclusionary rule. Explain how the independent source and inevitable discovery exceptions work.

answer.exemplar: The independent source exception admits evidence that the police would have obtained without the constitutional violation, such as a separate valid search conducted later for lawful reasons. Inevitable discovery admits evidence that a lawful procedure would have exposed anyway, and both require the government to prove by a preponderance that the evidence would have been found without the unconstitutional step.

questions.explanation: Both exceptions ask whether the evidence would have been obtained anyway through lawful means, and both place the burden on the government. The card example shows a separate lawful search producing the same evidence.
questions.hint: Ask whether the evidence was already available by law.

options.misconception: treats any warrant as curing the earlier defect

questions.topic: Voluntariness of consent to search
questions.learningObjective: Explain the treatment of a coerced consent claim
questions.stem: Study card 31 involves a detained driver who says he signed the consent form because officers told him he would be held overnight otherwise. Explain how the court should treat that claim.

answer.exemplar: The court applies a totality analysis to the circumstances of the encounter: the nature and duration of the detention, the presence or absence of advisements, the number and manner of questioning, and whether the officer made an express or implied promise. questions.explanation: Voluntariness is judged objectively under the totality of the circumstances, and an officer threat to detain is a powerful indicator of coercion. The government usually bears the burden of proving consent was free.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Searching a vehicle without a warrant
questions.learningObjective: Explain the reasoning behind the automobile exception
questions.stem: Study card 40 asks why the automobile exception permits a warrantless vehicle search. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The exception rests on two features: probable cause to believe the vehicle holds evidence of a crime, and the inherent mobility of a car, which creates a real risk that the evidence will be moved or destroyed before a warrant can issue. Courts treat the combination as justifying a search of the areas of the vehicle where such evidence might reasonably be found.

questions.explanation: Probable cause plus mobility is what permits the warrantless search, and the scope of that search is limited to places evidence might be. The rationale is practical, not a licence to search a vehicle exhaustively.
questions.hint: Focus on probable cause and the risk of loss.

questions.topic: Reliance on a defective warrant
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of good faith reliance
questions.stem: Study card 49 asks when officers may rely on a warrant even if it later turns out to be invalid. Explain the limits of that protection.

answer.exemplar: Officers are generally protected when they reasonably rely on a warrant that appears valid on its face, and the protection extends to facially deficient warrants so long as the defect is not so obvious that a reasonable officer would have known of it. The protection fails entirely where the affiant lied to the magistrate, or where the magistrate abandoned his role as a neutral reviewer.

questions.explanation: Good faith reliance covers apparently valid warrants and officers with no reason to suspect otherwise, and it fails where the affiant lied or the judge was not a neutral reviewer. The exceptions define the outer limit.

questions.explanation: Each exception branch requires the government to show lawful acquisition by another route, and the independent source branch is the clearest. Good faith is a limited defence, and later consent does not cure a past violation.
questions.hint: Ask what lawful route would have produced the evidence.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Openness of criminal trials
questions.learningObjective: Explain why trials are open
questions.stem: Study card 58 asks why courts distrust closed proceedings. Explain the reasoning that makes trials open.

answer.exemplar: Public trials and public attendance are matters of tradition and of suspicion of secrecy, and the public right of access is also grounded in the idea that the judiciary is a branch of government accountable to the people. Closure therefore requires a finding of exceptional need and a narrowly drawn order, because openness is the presumption and secrecy is the departure.

questions.explanation: Openness is the default because secret proceedings are hard to supervise and easy to abuse, and the public presence supports accountability. Closure requires findings and narrow tailoring rather than convenience.
questions.hint: Focus on accountability and the burden of proving closure.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The fruit of the poisonous tree and its exceptions
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of items free of suppression issues
questions.stem: Study card 59 lists 100 items of evidence: 12 were suppressed as fruit of an unconstitutional search, 8 were admitted under an exception, and the remainder faced no suppression issue. What percentage of the 100 items faced no suppression issue at all?
questions.explanation: One hundred minus 12 minus 8 leaves 80 items with no suppression issue, which is 80 percent. The figures show the exclusionary rule reaches a minority of evidence in this set.
questions.hint: Subtract both groups before taking the share.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The right to receive information
questions.learningObjective: Describe the structure of a strong access statute

stimulus.body: Section 2. Public records. Except as expressly provided by law, all records of public offices are public records and are available for inspection and copying during office hours. Any person may request any public record. A public office shall not withhold a record unless it identifies a specific exemption applicable to the record requested, and shall state the exemption in writing within five business days of the request.

questions.stem: Study card 60 reviews this statute against the access table. Which description best fits it?

options.text: A statute that lets offices withhold records at their own discretion
options.misconception: ignores the written exemption requirement

options.text: A statute that limits requests to those made for a stated commercial purpose
options.misconception: invents a purpose limitation the statute lacks

options.text: A statute that applies only to state agencies and not to local offices
options.misconception: narrows the statute scope without support

options.text: A strong access statute with an identified exemption requirement and a deadline

questions.explanation: The statute creates a broad presumption of access, requires the office to identify a specific exemption, and sets a deadline for the written response. That structure favours disclosure over discretionary withholding.
questions.hint: Read the duty to identify an exemption in writing.
